segments.t: Meanwhile, in the communal flat, Samson's wife Nina is furious: he went through with that silly, humiliating kiss for the mayor, and he still got no job. Last time, that same mayor, Arkady, was arrested in a café for taking a large bribe, and the news is about to reach the television in this little room. Let's listen in Russian first.
Ну, Ваня! Ты всё сделал, а работы нет.
А что ты кричишь?
Что я кричу? Я жить нормально хочу!
А что я мог сделать?
Надо было у него расписку взять.
Расписку? У мэра?
Да! Даже ребёнок знает.
Юля, иди уроки учи!
Ой, смотри! Новости.
Задержан мэр города Аркадий Аникеев.
Что? Наш Аркашка?
Суд решил: домашний арест по месту прописки.
По месту прописки? Это же здесь, у нас!
Новый мэр — заместитель Аникеева.
Вот это новости!
И работы нет, и мэра нет.
Let's take it slowly from the top. Nina speaks first, and she is not calm.
Ну, Ваня! Ты всё сделал, а работы нет.

'Oh, Vanya! You did everything, and there's no job.' In response, Vanya is the everyday form of Ivan, Samson's real name; Samson is only a nickname. The little word in the middle means 'and' with a hint of 'but': it sets up the contrast. Samson doesn't like her tone.
А что ты кричишь?
'Why are you shouting?' Literally, 'and what are you shouting?' In complaints like this, 'what' often does the job of 'why'. Nina throws the question straight back.
Что я кричу?
'Why am I shouting?' The same action word, now with 'I'. Then she gives the real reason.
Я жить нормально хочу!

'I want to live a normal life!' Word for word, 'I to live normally want'. Word order is loose in Russian: you can move words around for emphasis and the meaning stays the same. Samson tries to defend himself.
А что я мог сделать?
'And what could I do?' 'Could' is in the past, in the short form a man uses; a woman would add a syllable at the end. Nina knows exactly what he should have done.
Надо было у него расписку взять.

'You should have got a receipt from him.' The first two words together mean 'it was necessary', a handy way to say 'you should have'. A receipt here is a written note that proves a promise was made. Samson can hardly believe his ears.
Расписку? У мэра?
'A receipt? From the mayor?' After the little word for 'from', the mayor gets a new ending, the one that means 'of'. Nina has no doubts at all.
Да! Даже ребёнок знает.
'Yes! Even a child knows.' Their teenage daughter Yulia is listening in, and she clearly agrees. So Samson sends her off.
Юля, иди уроки учи!
'Yulia, go and do your homework!' Literally, 'go learn your lessons'. Two action words side by side with no 'and' between them, very natural in speech. Then Nina notices the television.
Ой, смотри! Новости.
'Oh, look! The news.' The word for news is plural, and it always talks about several pieces of news at once. And here comes the big story.
Задержан мэр города Аркадий Аникеев.

'The town's mayor, Arkady Anikeev, has been detained.' This is television language: the action word comes first, in a short formal form meaning 'detained'. It's the man who cheated Samson. Samson can't believe it.
Что? Наш Аркашка?

'What? Our Arkasha?' Right then, Arkasha, and this cheekier form of it, are what everyone called Arkady when he was a little boy in this very flat. 'Our' makes him one of the family again. The newsreader goes on.
Суд решил: домашний арест по месту прописки.

'The court has decided: house arrest at his registered address.' In Russia every person is officially registered at one address, and that phrase at the end means exactly that. Nina works it out first.
По месту прописки? Это же здесь, у нас!

'At his registered address? But that's here, at our place!' The short word after 'that' adds 'but, you know', and the last two words mean 'at our home'. Arkady never moved his registration out of the communal flat. And there's one more piece of news.
Новый мэр — заместитель Аникеева.
'The new mayor is Anikeev's deputy.' There's no 'is' in the present: a short dash does the job. The deputy is Pasha, the ambitious man we met at the town hall. Samson sums it up.
Вот это новости!
'Well, that's news!' Said with feeling, it means 'what a surprise'. And Nina has the last word.
И работы нет, и мэра нет.

'No job, and no mayor either.' Word for word, 'and of work there's none, and of mayor there's none'. After 'there is no', the missing thing takes the ending for 'of'. The double 'and' works like 'neither, nor'. Now let's hear the whole scene again, from the start.
Ну, Ваня! Ты всё сделал, а работы нет.
А что ты кричишь?
Что я кричу? Я жить нормально хочу!
А что я мог сделать?
Надо было у него расписку взять.
Расписку? У мэра?
Да! Даже ребёнок знает.
Юля, иди уроки учи!
Ой, смотри! Новости.
Задержан мэр города Аркадий Аникеев.
Что? Наш Аркашка?
Суд решил: домашний арест по месту прописки.
По месту прописки? Это же здесь, у нас!
Новый мэр — заместитель Аникеева.
Вот это новости!
И работы нет, и мэра нет.
And that's the scene: no job and no receipt for Samson, but the man who cheated him is about to move into the room next door. See you next time!
Пока!
